summary: This informational document defines Brotli, a lossless compressed data format that combines LZ77 with Huffman coding, with efficiency comparable to the best general-purpose compression methods available. The specification describes the format of the compressed data stream. It is widely used for compressing web content.

eli5.summary: Brotli is a way to pack a suitcase very tightly so it takes less room, and you can unpack it later with nothing missing. It finds repeated parts and writes them down in a shorter way.

subtitle: The compressed data format that combines LZ77, Huffman coding, context modeling and a built-in dictionary.

tldr.problem: General-purpose compression needs a portable format that is considerably better than gzip, decompresses much faster than current LZMA implementations, and works on streams with bounded memory.
tldr.mechanism: A brotli stream is a header plus meta-blocks. Each meta-block is a series of commands that insert literals and copy earlier data, or a word from a static dictionary, all written with Huffman-style prefix codes chosen by block type and context.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7932 is the authoritative specification of the format and registers the HTTP content coding br. It is Informational and has been updated by RFC 9841.

today: RFC 7932 is an Informational document that has been updated by RFC 9841. It registered br in the HTTP Content Coding Registry.

sections.title: Goals and Scope of the Format
sections.content:
RFC 7932 defines a lossless compressed data format. It is independent of CPU type, operating system, file system and character set, so it can be used for interchange. It can be produced or consumed for an arbitrarily long stream using only an a priori bounded amount of intermediate storage.

The stated aims are a compression ratio comparable to the best general-purpose methods, in particular considerably better than the gzip program, and decompression much faster than current LZMA implementations. It does not try to allow random access, or to compress specialized data such as raster graphics as densely as specialized algorithms.

The document is the authoritative specification: it defines the set of valid streams and a decoder algorithm. It reuses the notation of DEFLATE (RFC 1951), including the relevant text, and says the format is an integral part of WOFF File Format 2.0. All multi-byte numbers are stored least significant byte first, and data elements are packed starting from the least significant bit of each byte, with prefix codes packed starting from their most significant bit.
sections.eli5: Brotli is a recipe for squeezing files smaller. Anyone who follows the recipe can unsqueeze the file and get exactly the original back.

sections.title: Streams, Meta-Blocks and Commands
sections.content:
A compressed data set is a header followed by a series of meta-blocks. Each meta-block decompresses to 0 to 16,777,216 (16 MiB) bytes, and the output is their concatenation. The header holds the sliding window size, a power of two minus 16 with the power in the range 10 to 24. A decoder must keep at least that much earlier output.

Inside a meta-block, the compressed part is a series of commands. Each command inserts some literal bytes and then copies a string from earlier output, given as a pair of length and backward distance. The minimum copy length is two. A copy may instead refer to an entry in a static dictionary. Three kinds of prefix codes are used: one for combined insert-and-copy lengths, one for literals and one for distances.

A meta-block can also store its data uncompressed on byte boundaries, which cannot be the last meta-block, or be empty. An empty meta-block may carry metadata bytes that are not part of the window or the output.
sections.eli5: Brotli writes the file as a list of instructions: 'write these letters' and 'repeat what you wrote a while ago'. Repeating is much shorter than writing the same thing again.

sections.title: Prefix Codes, Distances and Lengths
sections.content:
Brotli uses canonical prefix codes, so a code is fully defined by the bit lengths of its symbols. A prefix code is written either as a simple code, with up to four symbols, or as a complex code whose lengths are themselves compressed with a prefix code. Length symbols 16 and 17 repeat the previous non-zero length or a zero length.

Distances use a pair of distance code and extra bits, controlled by two header parameters, NPOSTFIX (0 to 3) and NDIRECT (0 to 120). The first 16 distance symbols refer to the last four distances, with small adjustments such as last distance minus one. The ring buffer of last distances starts as 16, 15, 11 and 4.

Insert lengths and copy lengths share one alphabet of 704 insert-and-copy length codes, each with extra bits. Codes 0 to 127 imply that the last distance is reused, so no distance is stored. Block types (up to 256 per category) let the encoder switch to a different set of prefix codes mid-meta-block through block-switch commands.
sections.eli5: Common letters get short secret codes and rare letters get long ones, like using a single tap for 'e' and a long sequence for 'z'. Brotli also keeps a short list of recent jump sizes so it can say 'same as last time'.

sections.title: Context Modeling and the Static Dictionary
sections.content:
Which prefix code is used for a literal depends on the block type and on a context ID from 0 to 63, computed from the previous two bytes. There are four context modes: LSB6, MSB6, UTF8 and Signed. For distances the context is the copy length, giving IDs 0 to 3. A context map turns each block type and context ID into the index of a prefix code. It is stored with run-length coding of zeros and an optional inverse move-to-front transform.

If a decoded distance is larger than the allowed window or the data produced so far, it is a reference to a word in a static dictionary instead (Appendix A, 122,784 bytes). The copy length for such a reference must be between 4 and 24. Each dictionary word has 121 different forms produced by transformations such as omitting leading or trailing bytes or changing letter case, listed in Appendix B.
sections.eli5: Brotli looks at the last two letters to guess what comes next, so it can use a better code book. It also ships with a built-in book of common words, so it does not have to spell them out.

sections.title: Stream and Meta-Block Headers
sections.content:
The stream header has one field, WBITS, a value from 10 to 24 coded in 1 to 7 bits. The window size is (1 << WBITS) - 16.

Each meta-block header begins with ISLAST and, when that is set, ISLASTEMPTY. Then come MNIBBLES and MLEN - 1, the uncompressed length. Then ISUNCOMPRESSED when the block is not the last one. Next are the number of block types for literals, insert-and-copy lengths and distances, then NPOSTFIX and NDIRECT, a context mode for each literal block type, the two context maps and the prefix codes.

The data part is a sequence of commands in the order set out in section 9.3. Section 10 gives the complete decoding algorithm in pseudo-code. Invalid cases, for example a distance resolving to zero or a stream ending before the last meta-block is complete, mean the stream should be rejected.
sections.eli5: Each chunk begins with a label saying how big it is, whether it is the last one and which code books it uses. The decoder reads the label first, then the instructions.

sections.title: Compressor Notes and Security
sections.content:
Section 11 is not part of the format. It gives a trivial compressor that stores data uncompressed, which never shrinks the data but shows that N bytes always fit in at most N + (3 * (N >> 16) + 5) bytes. It also describes how to align meta-blocks to byte boundaries and create self-contained parts of a stream.

The security section warns that decompressors should handle any input, bounds-check every memory access derived from decoded values, and sanity-check the meta-block size and window size so that small inputs cannot cause disproportionate CPU, memory or storage use. Compressors should allocate at least the output size above or fall back to the trivial algorithm.

It also warns that mixing attacker-supplied data with secrets in one compressed stream, then observing the encrypted length, can let an attacker reconstruct the secret. Applications should not mix sensitive and non-sensitive data in the same compressed stream.
sections.eli5: A decoder must be careful with files that lie about how big they are, and should never pack secrets together with things a stranger can choose, because the size can leak hints.

data.title: Example meta-block with four commands
data.code:
IaC0 L0 L1 LBlockSwitch(1, 3) L2 D0 IaC1 DBlockSwitch(1, 3) D1
IaCBlockSwitch(1, 2) IaC2 L3 L4 D2 IaC3 LBlockSwitch(0, 1) L5 D3
